title: Health Insurance Amendment (National Rural Health Commissioner) Bill 2017
short_title: Health Insurance Amendment (National Rural Health Commissioner) Bill 2017

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would create a statutory National Rural Health Commissioner to improve rural health policies and support rural practice.
The Commissioner would develop a National Rural Generalist Pathway and work with governments and the health sector to enhance training and remuneration for rural generalists.
The bill would also repeal sections 19AD and 3GC of the Health Insurance Act 1973, ending a review process and the Medical Training Review Panel.
changes: Establishes the National Rural Health Commissioner as a statutory office holder.
Repeals section 19AD of the Health Insurance Act 1973, removing the requirement for five-yearly reviews of certain Medicare provider number provisions.
Repeals section 3GC of the Health Insurance Act 1973, abolishing the Medical Training Review Panel and transferring its functions to the National Medical Training Advisory Network.
summary.affected: Rural, regional and remote communities, the rural health workforce, doctors, and the health sector would be affected.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: The Australian government moved to establish the first National Rural Health Commissioner, a statutory position to advocate for regional, rural and remote communities, develop National Rural Generalist Pathways, and improve health access; the bill also repeals the Medical Training Review Panel and a burdensome five-year review requirement on Medicare provider number legislation.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: Labor supported the bill but argued it was inadequate, noting the National Rural Health Commissioner's position terminates in July 2020 without review, the role is narrowly focused on a rural generalist pathway, and there is no advisory body; Labor moved an amendment to broaden the commissioner's scope, add review provisions, and establish an advisory body.

speeches.speaker: Ted O'Brien
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Health Insurance Amendment (National Rural Health Commissioner) Bill 2017, which establishes a National Rural Health Commissioner with $4.4 million in funding, repeals redundant sections of the Health Insurance Act, and aims to improve rural healthcare workforce distribution through a national rural generalist pathway.

speeches.speaker: Damian Drum
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Health Insurance Amendment (National Rural Health Commissioner) Bill 2017, which establishes a statutory National Rural Health Commissioner for two years with $4.4 million in investment to identify and address gaps in rural and remote health services. The bill also repeals section 3GC of the Health Insurance Act to abolish the Medical Training Review Panel, and the speaker commended former minister Fiona Nash and current minister David Gillespie for advancing the initiative.

speeches.speaker: Ross Hart
speeches.brief: The Health Insurance Amendment (National Rural Health Commissioner) Bill 2017 establishes a national rural health commissioner to advise on rural generalist pathways and address health workforce shortages in rural and remote areas. Labor will not oppose the bill but will move Senate amendments to broaden the commissioner's role, review rather than cease the office on 1 July 2020, and establish an unpaid advisory board, while urging the government to fund organisations like Rural Alive and Well Tasmania.

speeches.speaker: Lucy Wicks
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Health Insurance Amendment (National Rural Health Commissioner) Bill 2017, which establishes a national rural health commissioner with $4.4 million in funding, and highlighted actions to address a GP shortage in the Peninsula region of the Robertson electorate, including changes to the District of Workforce Shortage system and a new collaboration with GP Synergy to increase registrar placements.

speeches.speaker: Warren Snowdon
speeches.brief: Labor supported the bill to establish a National Rural Health Commissioner but argued its role was too narrow, focused only on a rural generalist pathway, and that the position should not cease in 2020. The speaker called for the commissioner's scope to be broadened to include the full range of rural health workforce and service issues.

speeches.speaker: David Littleproud
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Health Insurance Amendment (National Rural Health Commissioner) Bill 2017, arguing it would improve rural health outcomes by establishing a commissioner to drive community-based solutions and training pathways, citing higher mortality rates and fewer medical practitioners in remote areas compared to cities.

speeches.speaker: Brian Mitchell
speeches.brief: Labor supported the bill for a National Rural Health Commissioner but argued the government’s role was too narrow, proposing amendments to broaden the commissioner’s scope, review rather than end the position by 1 July 2020, and create an unpaid advisory board. The member highlighted Tasmania’s low GP numbers, the highest mortality rates in Australia, and cuts to preventative rural health services as evidence of inadequate government action.

speeches.speaker: George Christensen
speeches.brief: The bill fulfils the 2016 election commitment to establish a National Rural Health Commissioner, funded with $4.4 million through June 2020, to develop a national rural generalist pathway and improve rural health outcomes, and repeals redundant sections 3GC and 19AD of the Health Insurance Act 1973.

speeches.speaker: John McVeigh
speeches.brief: The speaker strongly supported the Health Insurance Amendment (National Rural Health Commissioner) Bill 2017, arguing it would improve rural health outcomes by recruiting and retaining doctors and health professionals outside major cities. They noted $5.5 million in funding for Sunrise Way and other local agencies under the coalition government's ice strategy.

speeches.speaker: Michelle Landry
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Health Insurance Amendment (National Rural Health Commissioner) Bill, arguing it would bridge rural health gaps by establishing a commissioner to collaborate with local experts, attract rural generalists through incentives, and address disparities—noting 85% of specialists work in cities and GP ratios in major cities double those in remote areas.

speeches.speaker: Cathy McGowan
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Health Insurance Amendment (National Rural Health Commissioner) Bill 2017 as a first step but argued it lacks ambition, announcing amendments to require the minister to table the commissioner's final report within five sitting days, mandate consultation with rural communities, and include consideration of no-gap bulk-billing affordability.

speeches.speaker: Rowan Ramsey
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Health Insurance Amendment (National Rural Health Commissioner) Bill 2017 and its $4.4 million budget allocation, but argued that rural health facilities in South Australia—such as those in Quorn, Jamestown, and Yorketown—are being neglected by the state government. He proposed postcode-specific Medicare provider numbers to address doctor shortages in rural areas, warning that without reform, Australia will face chronic overservicing in cities and worsening shortages in the country.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: The Health Insurance Amendment (National Rural Health Commissioner) Bill 2017 delivers on a 2016 election promise by establishing a Rural Health Commissioner, whose first priority is developing a rural generalist medical pathway, with additional responsibilities for nursing, allied health, Indigenous health, and other sectors. The commissioner will work with an existing rural stakeholder round table and a new distribution working group to address workforce challenges.
